clue.text: Terrific temper in children's 'entertainer'?

parts.note: a gleeful exclamation meaning 'terrific!', the kind shouted at a party

explanation.surface: A child throws a tremendous tantrum at a party, right in front of the hired entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temper' looks like a noun, a fit of rage, and is a verb: to soften. The quotation marks round 'entertainer' warn that no person is meant but a joke-shop prank, the theme of the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A whoopee cushion makes a rude noise when sat on, which keeps children amused.

clue.text: Musician, 'experienced' performer ultimately, one inspired by voodoo?

definitions.text: Musician, 'experienced' performer ultimately, one inspired by voodoo?

parts.note: a hex is a voodoo curse; it goes round the rest

indicators.note: takes the final letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: last letters of musiciaN, experienceD, performeR

explanation.surface: A description of a guitarist whose music drew on the supernatural.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: Jimi Hendrix led The Jimi Hendrix Experience and recorded 'Voodoo Child', hence the quoted 'experienced' and the voodoo.
explanation.definitionFit: Jimi Hendrix was the musician behind the band The Experience and the song 'Voodoo Child'.

clue.text: One's stopped primate achieving good promotion

parts.note: an orang is an orangutan; its G comes off the end
g = good, promoted to sit inside OR_AN

explanation.surface: A monkey has been halted in its tracks just as it was due to be promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's stopped' is the definition: an organ has stops, the knobs that choose its voices. In a down clue promotion lifts G higher up the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ is played with stops, so it is a thing that is stopped.

clue.text: Open wound so deep, ten cuts

indicators.note: wound as in twisted, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor notes an open wound, deep and with ten cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' reads as an injury and is the past tense of wind: twisted. 'Open' is the adjective, as a wound left exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open is exposed to view or to the air.

clue.text: See 1
Only good uniform required to turn up for concert

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up lifts the letters so they read bottom to top

parts.note: U is uniform in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A dress code for a concert: only a good uniform will do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only good' has to be read as a phrase, a person with no sin. 'Required' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To act in unison is to act in concert, all together.

clue.text: In shock, if I'd run off with hero

indicators.note: off as in gone bad, so the letters are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone imagines their shock if they had run away with their hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run off' reads as eloping, but 'run' is only R and 'off' is the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: horror is the shock felt at something dreadful.

clue.text: Short catchy phrase arising, singing well!

indicators.note: HOOK is cut short, losing its last letter
in a down clue, the letters rise and read upwards

parts.note: a hook is a catchy phrase in a song; HOOK is cut to HOO

explanation.surface: A songwriter's note on a snappy chorus that sings nicely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well!' is an exclamation of surprise, the job 'ooh la la' does. A hook is the catchy line of a pop song.
explanation.definitionFit: Ooh la la is an exclamation of surprised delight, like 'well!'.

clue.text: Keen, with crush on children's 'entertainer'?

parts.note: to powder is to crush; 'with' just adds it

explanation.surface: Someone keen and besotted, with a crush on the party entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crush' looks like infatuation and is a verb: to grind to powder. Itching powder is a joke-shop prank, like the other quoted 'entertainers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Itching powder is a prank sprinkled down someone's back, a staple of children's joke shops.

clue.text: Somewhat passionless, no great show of affection

indicators.note: only some of the words' letters are used

explanation.surface: A lukewarm romance: rather passionless, with little affection shown.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface denies passion while hiding a passionate answer. A snog is British slang for a long kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a long, lingering kiss, about the most public display of fondness there is.

clue.text: Right manner the wrong way in incoherent arrangement favouring men

indicators.note: the letters run backwards
'in' places one thing inside another, so the reversed letters sit inside the word for incoherent

explanation.surface: A complaint that an arrangement tilted toward men is both wrong-headed and incoherent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a political argument and 'Right' looks like the political right; it is only R.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriarchy is a social order that gives power to men.

clue.text: God you are, but according to rumour?

indicators.note: rumour is what is heard said, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: you are = you're; but, heard as butt, is the backside

explanation.surface: An insult: you may be a god, but people talk.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the old schoolyard one: said aloud, Uranus sounds like 'your anus'. Uranus was the Greek god of the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Uranus was the primordial Greek sky god, father of the Titans.

clue.text: Tough with bug, I can hope initially to recover

indicators.note: takes the first letter of hope
to re-cover the ground is to go back over it, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to bug someone is to nag them
can is slang for the toilet, the loo

explanation.surface: A patient with a nasty bug hopes to get better soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough' looks like an adjective and is a noun: a tough is a thug. 'Can' and 'loo' are both slang for the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough, a violent young man, is a hooligan.

clue.text: Smoke bomb has old, old pig racing around

indicators.note: the letters are sent all around, rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd scene of an elderly pig tearing round with a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoke bomb' is a cigar (a smoke) that is also a bomb. The first 'old' gives EX; the second is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploding cigar is a smoke rigged to go off in the smoker's face, a classic prank.

clue.text: Crooked, skewed clear sense

indicators.note: bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that clear sense has been bent and twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked' means dishonest, not bent in shape, and 'nous' is British informal for good sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Larcenous means thieving, and a thief is crooked.

clue.text: See 14
See 25 Down
Constant protection of one aquatic bird by another, the first flying away

indicators.note: a bird flying away departs, so the first letter departs from the word

parts.note: a teal is a duck; it goes round the tern, then loses its T

explanation.surface: Nature notes: one waterbird shelters another until the first flies off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The first' means the first letter, not the first bird: TETERNAL drops its T.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal things are constant, never changing or ending.

clue.text: Program termination, time for add-on

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A software note: when a program closes, it's time for an extension.
explanation.walkthrough: The computing surface makes 'add-on' look like a plug-in, when it is any attached part.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendage is something added on or attached to a larger thing.

clue.text: Sea, in waves, within which to land

indicators.note: TO goes within the rearranged letters
the letters roll about like waves

explanation.surface: Sailors searching for somewhere to come ashore in heavy seas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land' reads as the verb, to come ashore, and is the noun: a country. Estonia does lie on the Baltic Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Land in the sense of a country, as in a foreign land; this one is a Baltic state.

clue.text: Children's entertainer faced misery, advance rebuffed by young ladies

parts.note: a misery is a grumpy person, a grouch

explanation.surface: A party entertainer, faced with a sulky crowd, has his approaches turned down by girls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faced' belongs to the definition: these are worn on the face. 'Misery' is British informal for a gloomy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Groucho glasses, fake specs with a big nose and moustache after Groucho Marx, are a joke-shop disguise worn on the face.

clue.text: Feeble grade in the end, fail with honour

indicators.note: only the final letter of grade is used

parts.note: to fete is to honour; 'with' adds it

explanation.surface: A weak student ends up failing, though with some honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The exam surface makes 'grade' and 'fail' look like one idea; each gives its own letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means weak and feeble, lacking vigour.

clue.text: Temperature only two or three in herb

parts.note: to run a temperature is to have a fever

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy that lowers a temperature by only a couple of degrees.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, feverfew was long taken as a remedy for fevers.
explanation.definitionFit: Feverfew is a daisy-like herb used in folk medicine.

clue.text: Film panned by liberal left, now showing

indicators.note: free with the letters, so they are rearranged

parts.note: a film now showing is on

explanation.surface: A film review: slated by left-wing critics, but now in cinemas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film panned' is no movie but a coating put on pans; 'panned' looks like a bad review. 'Liberal' and 'left' play at politics.
explanation.definitionFit: Teflon is the non-stick film coating the inside of frying pans.

clue.text: Dubious hair faced, safe balder anyhow

indicators.note: the letters are put in any old order

explanation.surface: A balding man thinks growing facial hair is the safer choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faced' belongs to the definition: the dubious hair is on the face.
explanation.definitionFit: A false beard is fake facial hair, a joke-shop disguise.

clue.text: Fun breaking rocks, even surprising

indicators.note: FUN is broken up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: e'en is the poetic contraction of even

explanation.surface: A children's game of smashing stones turns out to be surprisingly fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking rocks' looks like one action; 'breaking' works only on FUN, and 'rocks' stands on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what nobody saw coming takes people by surprise.

clue.text: Wet bit

definitions.meaning: a verb: to moisten with the tongue
a small amount, as of paint

explanation.walkthrough: A lick of paint is a bit of it, and to lick is to wet. Both words look like adjective and noun until read as verb and quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: To lick is to wet with the tongue, and a lick is a small amount.

clue.text: See 21 Down
Children's 'entertainer' given a poke, for not entirely crappy?

indicators.note: FOR loses its last letter
shoddy, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A prank toy gets prodded to check whether it is really as disgusting as it looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crappy' does double duty: the anagram instruction, and a knowing nod to what the answer imitates.
explanation.definitionFit: Fake poo is a joke-shop plastic turd, left about to shock people.
